notes.meaning: As Jesus walked along after leaving the temple, He saw a beggar who had been blind since birth. This man could not see Jesus, but Jesus noticed him and showed pity. It was an impossible condition for human doctors to cure, which gave Christ an opportunity to show His power.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars see the man born blind as a symbol of all humanity, which is spiritually blind from birth.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition notes that every person is born blind in mind because sin took root in human nature.

notes.meaning: The disciples asked Jesus who had sinned to cause the blindness, the man himself or his parents. People in that culture often assumed that severe suffering was always the direct punishment for a specific evil deed. They wondered how someone could be born blind unless sin happened before birth or in the family.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars point out the common Jewish idea that all suffering came from sin, including ancient rabbinic teachings that an unborn baby could sin while still in the womb.

notes.meaning: Jesus made clear that neither the man's sin nor his parents' sin caused this blindness. Instead, the condition existed so that God could display His mighty works through him. Jesus warned His followers not to assume that terrible trouble is proof of special guilt.

differ.view: Christians in this tradition teach that God ordained this affliction from the start for the sovereign purpose of displaying His glory through the cure.
Christians in this tradition teach that Jesus refused to answer curious questions about the cause of evil, stating only that this specific affliction was not a penalty for sin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note the Greek wording can mean either that God purposed the blindness for this end or that He used the outcome for His glory, since nothing falls outside God's sovereign care.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic writers explain that while every person shares in original sin, this disability was not sent as a personal punishment.

notes.meaning: Jesus urged His followers to carry out the Father's work while the light lasts. Day represents a person's lifetime of opportunity, while night points to death when earthly labor must end. Because His earthly ministry would soon finish, Jesus worked with urgency to do good.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars explain that the word 'must' shows divine necessity, and the coming 'night' points directly to Jesus departing from the world.

notes.meaning: Jesus declared that while He was in the world, He was the light of the world. Just as the sun brightens the physical earth, Jesus gives spiritual understanding and life to human souls. He brought both physical sight to blind eyes and divine truth to dark hearts.

Jesus spat on the ground, mixed the saliva with dirt to form mud, and spread it on the man's eyes. He used simple, unlikely means that might normally blind a seeing person to show that God works in unexpected ways. His action also challenged human traditions that forbade making paste or applying remedies on the Sabbath.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching often follows Augustine in seeing the mud made of dirt and saliva as a sign of the divine Word taking on human flesh.

notes.meaning: Jesus ordered the man to go and wash in the pool of Siloam, a name meaning 'Sent.' The man trusted Christ's word, washed in the water, and came back fully able to see. The pool pointed to Jesus Himself, the Messiah sent by the Father to bring healing to the world.

differ.view: Christians in this tradition emphasize that the healing occurred only when the man took an active step of obedient faith.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition views the washing in the pool of Siloam as a picture of Christian baptism, which brings spiritual light to those who believe.

notes.meaning: Neighbors and people who had often seen the man begging were astonished to see him with sight. He was a familiar figure at the city gates, so his lifelong blindness was widely known. His public life meant there could be no doubt about his previous condition.

People in the crowd argued over whether he was really the same man or just someone who looked like him. The sudden gift of sight had changed his appearance so much that some doubted their own eyes. The man settled the debate himself by speaking up and confirming that he was indeed the beggar.
The neighbors asked the man how his eyes had been opened. They did not deny the wonderful fact that he could now see, but they wanted to understand how such a miracle was performed.

The man gave a direct, truthful account of what had happened. He explained that a man called Jesus put mud on his eyes, told him to wash at Siloam, and that his sight came as soon as he obeyed. At this point, the man knew Jesus only by name and had not yet seen Him with his own eyes.
The people asked where Jesus was, but the man had to admit he did not know. Jesus had quietly walked away after sending the man to the pool, so the healed man had never seen his healer.

The neighbors brought the healed man to the Pharisees, who were the recognized religious leaders and judges. They probably wanted an official ruling on whether a genuine miracle had taken place and whether any laws had been broken.

The healing took place on the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest. Strict religious tradition forbade kneading clay or applying medicine to eyes on the holy day. Jesus chose this day on purpose to show that works of mercy and necessity do not violate God's law.

The Pharisees began their own investigation by asking the man how he had received his sight. The man repeated his short, clear story, telling them that Jesus put mud on his eyes, he washed, and now he could see.

Some Pharisees argued that Jesus could not be from God because He broke their rules for the Sabbath. Other leaders objected, asking how an ungodly impostor could perform such powerful, good signs. This sharp disagreement created a deep split among the rulers.

The Pharisees turned back to the healed man to ask what he thought of the person who gave him sight. The man spoke up with courage and declared that Jesus was a prophet sent by God. Even with his limited knowledge, the man recognized that divine power was at work.

The hostile rulers refused to accept that the man had ever been blind at all. They suspected fraud because admitting the miracle would mean admitting Jesus' divine authority. To test the story, they summoned the man's parents for questioning.

The leaders questioned the parents with demanding queries to see if they were telling the truth. They asked if the man was really their son, if he was truly born blind, and how he was now able to see. Their sharp tone was meant to intimidate the parents into backing down.

The parents answered firmly that he was indeed their son and that he had been born blind. They knew this from years of sorrow and caring for him from infancy. Their plain testimony destroyed the leaders' claim that the blindness was fake.
